messages.author: 280ac6f65b06d396
messages.subject: Evasive movement?
parts:
I performed winter point counts using playback for Bachman's sparrows.
I had the highest number of responses occur 20-30 meters from the point.
Therefore my data lacks the "shoulder" at 0 and instead occurs in the
20-30m interval. This implies that there is evasive movement or there
is simply lower response frequency within 20-30m perhaps because the
birds are "scared" of the playback. I had more than 125 registrations
on each of two separate study sites(total ~250). I am considering
setting the 20-30 meter interval as my "zero" then calculating the
densities to the "right" and then doing the same thing to the "left" and
adding the densities. I have two questions 1) will this generate a
valid estimate? and 2) how do you add the variances if this can be done?
thanks,
clark jones

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Evasive movement?
parts:
Clark-

Evasive movement is much less problematic than attractive movement in
generating bias. However, I'm not sure you have evasive movement. With
point count data, a histogram of distances will have the interval with
the highest count at some distance from zero. That is because the area
represented by the distance interval is increasing with the square of
distance (ie area of circle = pi*r*r). At the same time the detection
probability decreases with distance, so the resulting histogram of
distances will increase and then decline. I don't have the Intro
distance sampling book in front of me but I believe there is an
illustration of that in the book. That is why fit of the data to point
count is shown in 2 plots. One shows the histogram of observed
distances as I've described and the other shows that histogram scaled to
represent a detection function which should have a shoulder. You can
think about this latter histogram as representing observed distance in
each of the concentric rings represented by the distance intervals. If
your email refers to this latter histogram you may have evasive movement
but I would not jump to that conclusion. First I'd look at the
chi-square test to see if it suggested a lack of fit near distance 0.
Because the first distance interval represents a small area there is
much more variation in the number seen in that interval and a low number
does not imply a lack of fit necessarily. Now if there is a lack of
fit, then you may want to consider evasive movement or other
explanations. You offered 2 possible explanations and I'll offer a
third. The best analytical solution will depend on the cause of the
problem. If birds are scared and do not respond at close distance, then
your suggestion to truncate at 20-30m is the best way to go. If
however, it is evasive movement and birds are moving from the close
interval to the 20-30m bin and then calling/seen, then you don't want to
truncate and you should fit the data as they are because it will smooth
those counts that are too high in the 20-30m bin and too low in the <20m
bin because of the evasive movement. If you want further explanation of
that look back to the Wildlife Monograph of Burnham et al 1980 on line
transect sampling. Now for a third possibility. You are using playback
methods which I believe are fraught with problems. See the work by
Klavitter on playback point counts with Hawaiian hawks. I submit that
it may be just as likely that the bird is being attracted and that you
are first seeing them in the 20-30 m interval and they may represent
birds that were originally much further away. This is a much more
insidious problem. I submit that the only way you'll reconcile which is
the cause and the solution is to put transmitters on a sample of birds
and approach at various distances like the work of Klavitter.

Hope this helps.

--jeff

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Evasive movement?
parts:
Further to Jeff's message (thanks Jeff), Steve Buckland and others have a
paper coming out in Journal of Applied Ecology about the use of playback
experiments in a distance-sampling-like framework. A copy is on my web site
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/
under "Publications and preprints", and I've pasted the abstract below.

- Len

Buckland, S.T., R.W. Summers, D.L. Borchers and L. Thomas. Point transect
sampling with traps or lures. Journal of Applied Ecology.

Summary
1. The ability to monitor abundance of animal populations is becoming
increasingly important, in light of growing concerns over the loss of
biodiversity through anthropogenic changes. A widely-used tool for such
monitoring is distance sampling, in which distances of detected animals from
a line or point are modelled, to estimate detectability and hence abundance.
Nevertheless, many species still prove problematic to survey. We develop two
extensions to point transect sampling that potentially allow abundance to be
estimated of a number of species from diverse taxa for which good survey
methods have not previously been available.
2. For each method, the primary survey comprises a random sample of points,
or more usually a systematic grid of points, through the region of interest.
Animals are lured to a point, or trapped at a point, and the number of
animals observed at each point is recorded. A separate study is conducted on
a subset of animals, to record whether they respond to the lure or enter the
trap, for a range of known distances from the point. These data are used to
estimate the probability that an animal will respond to the lure or enter
the trap, as a function of its initial distance from the point. This allows
the counts to be converted to an estimate of abundance in the survey region.
3. We illustrate the methods using a lure survey of crossbills Loxia spp. in
coniferous woodland in Scotland.
4. Synthesis and applications. Two extensions of point transect sampling
that use the same statistical methodology, lure point transects and trapping
point transects, are developed. Lure point transects extend the
applicability of distance sampling to species that can be lured to a point,
while trapping point transects potentially allow abundance estimation of
species that can be trapped, with fewer resources than are required by
trapping webs or conventional mark-recapture methods.

Key-words: distance sampling, logistic regression, Loxia scotica, lure point
transects, point transect sampling, trapping point transects, trapping webs
